Introduction

Snakes and Ladders is a simple board game originating from Ancient India, in which two or more players race to traverse a board. In assignment 2, you will create a simplified version of Snakes and Ladders. This prototype will be a one player game and will be text based. We will also be adding magic potions.

Getting Started

Download a2.zip from Blackboard. This archive contains the necessary files to start your assignment. Once extracted, the a2.zip archive will provide the following files:

  • a2.py: This is the only file where you write your code and is the only .py file you will submit. Do not make changes to any other files.
  • support.py: Do not modify or submit this file, it contains pre-defined constants to use in your assignment. In addition to these, you are encouraged to create your own constants in a2.py where possible.
  • level1.txt: An example file for a level. You will need to be able to read and load this level for later tasks. Your finished program will also need to be able to load any text file conforming to this sort of layout. Do not submit this file.
  • gameplay/: This folder contains a number of example outputs generated by playing the game using a fully-functional completed solution to this assignment. The purpose of the files in this folder is to help you understand how the game works, and how output should be formatted.

If you also wish to download this task sheet you must first click View Fullscreen at the top of the page. This will open the task sheet in a new browser tab. On this tab, use Ctrl-PCtrl-P to print the page, and select Save to PDF as the output location. The print button on Blackboard only captures the first two or so pages of this sheet (a limitation of Blackboard beyond our control).

Gameplay

This section provides a high-level overview of gameplay, and is intended to provide you with an idea of the behaviour of a fully completed assignment. Where interactions are not explicitly mentioned in this section, please see the Implementation section.

Important

Do not simply implement the behaviour described here using your own structure; you must implement the individual functions, classes, and methods described in the Implementation section. Inputs and outputs must match exactly what is expected. Refer to the Implementation section, the given examples, and the provided Gradescope tests for clarification on required prompts and outputs.

In Snake Game, a player starts with a given amount of health and a given number of remaining rolls. In each turn , the player rolls a dice and moves along a path, which is made up of tiles. The player moves by the number of steps indicated by the dice roll. Tiles may be a floor, or an exit. There are also a number of entities that exist on the path. The player is themselves an entity. Other entities include snakes, ladders and various types of potions.

The objective of the game is for the player to reach the exit at the end of the path. The player must land precisely on the exit. For example, if the player is two steps away from the exit and rolls a three, they cannot move and must try again on their next turn. Each dice roll uses one of the player’s remaining rolls.

As the player moves along the path, they may step on snakes, ladders or potions. If the player lands on a snake, they lose one point of health and are sent back to the start of the path. If the player lands on a potion, the potion’s effect is applied to the player and the potion is then removed from the game. If the player lands on a ladder, they are moved forward along the path by the number of steps specified by the ladder’s length.

The path is rectangular in shape and has an alternating pattern. For example, the path below has five rows and three columns:

Potions are collectable entities which have a number of effects that can be applied to increase a player’s health and/or number of remaining rolls, thereby allowing the player to complete games they may otherwise be unable to complete. When the player moves onto a position containing a potion, the potion’s effects are applied to the player and the potion is then removed from the game. Each effect is applied with a value, which determines the strength of the effect. The behavior of each effect is described in Table 1.

After starting a Snake Game, a welcome message is displayed, and the following game loop is then repeated:

  1. At each turn, the game state is printed to the screen and the player is prompted to press Enter to roll the dice. Once the player presses Enter, the dice is rolled, the result of roll is displayed on the screen, and one of the player’s remaining rolls is consumed.
  2. The player is moved along the path by the number of steps indicated by the dice roll. If this move would take the player beyond the exit, a message is displayed indicating the number of steps required to reach the exit. The player is not moved, the turn ends, and the game returns to Step 1.
  3. If the player moves and lands on an entity, the corresponding action is performed as described in Table 2. After the action is completed, the turn then ends, and the game returns to Step 1 for the next turn. The game loop continues until one of the following conditions occurs:
  • The player wins by reaching the exit at the end of the path.
  • The player loses by running out of remaining rolls before reaching the exit, or by running out of health.

Once the game is over, the final game state is displayed and the player is informed whether they won or lost. The program then terminates gracefully.

Required Classes and Methods

This section outlines the classes and methods you are required to implement in a2.py. Your program must operate exactly as specified. In particular, your program’s output must match exactly with the expected output. Your program will be marked automatically so minor differences in output (such as whitespace or casing) will cause tests to fail resulting in zero marks for that test.

The class diagram in Figure 2 provides an overview of all of the classes you must implement in your assignment, and the basic relationships between them. The details of these classes and their methods are described in depth later in this section. Within Figure 2:

  • Orange classes are those provided to you in the supporting files.
  • Green classes are abstract classes (superclasses). However, you are not required to enforce the abstract nature of the green classes in their implementation. The purpose of this distinction is to indicate to you that you should only ever instantiate the blue classes in your program (though you should instantiate the green classes to test them before beginning work on their subclasses).
  • Blue classes are concrete classes (subclasses).
  • Solid arrows indicate inheritance (i.e. the “is-a” relationship).
  • Dotted arrows indicate composition (i.e. the “has-a” relationship). An arrow marked with 1-1 denotes that each instance of the class at the base of the arrow contains exactly one instance of the class at the head of the arrow. An arrow marked with 1-n denotes that each instance of the class at the head of the arrow may contain many instances of the class at the tail of the arrow.
Note

You are awarded marks for the number of tests passed by your classes when they are tested independently of one another. Thus an incomplete assignment with some working classes may well be awarded more marks than a complete assignment with faulty classes.

Each class is accompanied with some examples for usage to help you start your own testing. You should also test your methods with other values to ensure they operate according to the descriptions.

Task 1 Tile()

Tile is an abstract class from which all instantiated types of tile inherit. This class provides default tile behavior, which can be inherited or overridden by specific types of tile. All tiles are given a single character identifier representing their type.

Abstract tiles have type representation T.

Tile must implement the following methods:

  • __str__(self) -> str
    Returns the single character representing this tile. Unless otherwise specified, this will be the tile’s type representation.
  • __repr__(self) -> str
    Returns a string which could be copied and pasted into a REPL to construct a new instance identical to self.
  • get_type(self) -> str Returns the single character representing the type of this tile.

Example:

>>> tile = Tile()
>>> tile
Tile()
>>> str(tile)
'T'
>>> tile.get_type()
'T'

Task 2 Floor(Tile)

Floor is a tile representing empty space on which entities can freely move. Floor tiles are given a type identifier of a full stop (.).

Example:

>>> tile = Floor()
>>> tile
Floor()
>>> str(tile)
'.'
>>> tile.get_type()
'.'

Task 3 Exit(Tile)

Exit is a tile representing the end of the path. Exits are represented by the character X.

Example:

>>> tile = Exit()
>>> tile
Exit()
>>> str(tile)
'X'
>>> tile.get_type()
'X'

Task 4 Entity()

Entity is an abstract class from which all instantiated types of entity inherit. This class provides default entity behavior, which can be inherited or overridden by specific types of entity. Each entity occupies a position. Positions are represented as (row, column) integer tuples, where (0, 0) denotes the top-left corner of the board. Like tiles, each entity is given a single character identifier representing its type. Base entities have type representation E.

Entity must implement the following methods:

  • __init__(self, position: tuple[int, int])
    Instantiate a new entity at the given position.
  • __repr__(self) -> str
    Returns a string which could be copied and pasted into a REPL to construct a new instance identical to self.
  • __str__(self) -> str Returns the single character representing this entity. Unless otherwise specified, this will be the entity’s type representation.
  • get_type(self) -> str Returns the single character representing the type of this entity.
  • get_position(self) -> tuple[int, int]
    Returns this entity’s position.
  • set_position(self, new_pos: tuple[int, int])
    Sets this entity’s position to the specified value.

Example:

>>> entity = Entity((0,1))
>>> entity
Entity((0, 1))
>>> str(entity)
'E'
>>> entity.get_type()
'E'
>>> entity.get_position()
(0, 1)
>>> entity.set_position((6,7))
>>> entity
Entity((6, 7))
>>> entity.get_position()
(6, 7)

Task 5 Potion(Entity)

A Potion is an abstract class which provides a simple interface which all instances of potions must implement.

Abstract potions have type representation O and no effects.

In addition to the Entity methods that must be supported, Potion must implement the following methods:

  • get_effect(self) -> dict[str, int]
    Returns this potion’s effect.

Example:

>>> potion = Potion((0,1))
>>> potion
Potion((0, 1))
>>> str(potion)
'O'
>>> potion.get_type()
'O'
>>> potion.get_position()
(0, 1)
>>> potion.get_effect()
{}

A HealthPotion is a sour tasting potion that increases the player’s health by 1. Health potions have the type representation H.

Example:

HealthPotion((0, 1))

'H'

'H'

Task 7 RollPotion(Potion)

A RollPotion is a fruity tasting potion that provides the player with 3 additional rolls. Roll potions have the type representation R.

Example:

>>> potion = RollPotion((0,1))
>>> potion
RollPotion((0, 1))
>>> str(potion)
'R'

'R'

(0, 1)

{'rolls': 3}

Task 8 FancyPotion(Potion)

A FancyPotion increases the player’s health by 2 and their remaining rolls by 2 (Very Fancy). Fancy Potions have the type representation F.

Note

It’s unclear what Fancy Potions taste like. Many people claim they taste like White Monster, however there’s an opposing camp who argue the taste is closer to La Croix.

Example:

>>> potion = FancyPotion((0,1))
>>> potion
FancyPotion((0, 1))
>>> str(potion)
'F'
>>> potion.get_type()
'F'
>>> potion.get_position()
(0, 1)
>>> potion.get_effect()
{'health': 2, 'rolls': 2}

Task 9 Snake(Entity)

A Snake is an entity that sits on the board and is represented by S.

Note

The Snake class should not handle the damage caused to a player who lands on a snake. Instead, this interaction should be handled by the SnakeGameModel class, which is responsible for managing interactions between entities.

Example:

>>> snake = Snake((0,1))
>>> snake
Snake((0, 1))
>>> str(snake)
'S'
>>> snake.get_type()
'S'
>>> snake.get_position()
(0, 1)

Task 10 Ladder(Entity)

A Ladder is an entity that sits on the board and is represented by L. Players who step on Ladders will be moved forwards a given number of places.

To support this extended functionality, the __init__ method of Ladder takes in an additional argument. In addition to the Entity methods that must be supported, Ladder must implement the following methods:

  • __init__(self, position: tuple[int, int], length: int)
    Instantiate a new ladder of specified length at the given position.
  • __str__(self) -> str
    Returns a string containing this ladder’s length.
  • get_length(self) -> int
    Returns this ladder’s length.

Example:

>>> ladder = Ladder((0,1), 6)
>>> ladder
Ladder((0, 1), 6)
>>> str(ladder)
'6'
>>> ladder.get_type()
'L'
>>> ladder.get_position()
(0, 1)
>>> ladder.get_length()
6

Task 11 Player(Entity)

Player denotes the entity directly controlled by the player. Player entities possess both a health value and a number of remaining rolls. These values may change throughout gameplay. Player instances have the type identifier P.

To support this extended functionality, The __init__ method of Player takes in two additional arguments. In addition to the Entity methods that must be supported, Player must implement the following methods:

  • __init__(self, position: tuple[int, int], health: int, remaining_rolls: int) Instantiate a new player at the given position, with the specified health and remaining rolls.
  • get_health(self) -> int
    Return this player’s current health.
  • add_health(self, amount: int)
    Add the given amount to this player’s health.
  • get_remaining_rolls(self) -> int
    Return the number of remaining rolls this player has.
  • add_remaining_rolls(self, rolls: int)
    Add the given number of rolls to the remaining rolls of this player instance.
  • apply_effect(self, effect: dict[str, int])
    Apply the given potion’s effects to this player.
  • has_finished(self) -> bool

Indicates whether this player has finished traversing the board. - finish(self) Signal to this instance that it has finished traversing the board. - is_alive(self) -> bool Indicates whether this instance of the player is alive. - has_remaining_rolls(self) -> bool Indicates whether this player has any remaining rolls.

Example:

>>> player = Player((0,1), 4, 2)
>>> player
Player((0, 1), 4, 2)
>>> str(player)
'P'
>>> player.get_type()
'P'
>>> player.get_position()
(0, 1)
>>> player.get_health()
4
>>> player.add_health(1)
>>> player
Player((0, 1), 5, 2)
>>> player.get_health()
5
>>> player.is_alive()
True
>>> player.add_health(-10)
>>> player.is_alive()
False
>>> player.get_remaining_rolls()
2
>>> player.add_remaining_rolls(2)
>>> player
Player((0, 1), -5, 4)
>>> player.get_remaining_rolls()
4
>>> player.has_remaining_rolls()
True
>>> player.add_remaining_rolls(-4)
>>> player.has_remaining_rolls()
False
>>> player.has_finished()
False
>>> player.finish()
>>> player.has_finished()
True
>>> player.apply_effect({})
>>> player
Player((0, 1), -5, 0)
>>> player.get_health()
-5
>>> player.get_remaining_rolls()
0
>>> player.apply_effect({
    'health': 6,
    'rolls': 2
})
>>> player
Player((0, 1), 1, 2)
>>> player.get_health()
1
>>> player.get_remaining_rolls()
2

Task 12 read_file(board_file: str) -> tuple[list[Tile], list[Entity], Player]

read_file is a helpful function that loads the tiles, entities, and player comprising a Snake Game from a text file.

You may assume that the file specified by board_file contains exactly the following:

  • A single line containing exactly two integers, corresponding to the player’s health and remaining moves in that order. This is followed immediately by:
  • A rectangular grid of single characters, denoting the board and the entities contained within it.

Within the rectangular grid, the character at each position is the string representation of the tile at that position on the board. If there is an entity at a given position on the board, the character at that position in the grid is instead the string representation of that entity. You may (and indeed must) assume that all entities present on the board are located on Floor tiles.

The list of entities that you return should not include the player entity, and should be ordered by entity position: from top to bottom with ties being broken from left to right.

Tip

level1.txt is an example of files that this function is expected to parse

Example:

>>> tiles, entities, player = read_file('levels/level1.txt')
>>> tiles
[[Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Exit()]]
>>> entities
[HealthPotion((0, 3)),
 Snake((1, 1)),
 Ladder((1, 3), 3),
 RollPotion((2, 2)),
 Snake((2, 4)),
 Ladder((3, 0), 4),
 FancyPotion((3, 1))]
>>> player
Player((0, 0), 3, 15)

Task 13 Path()

A Path abstracts the route that the player must follow through the board. Its responsibility is to handle the translation between one-dimensional path positions and two-dimensional board positions (see the figure provided in the Gameplay Section).

This assignment is not prescriptive about internal representation of path (within reason, of course), however a Path must support the following interface:

  • __init__(self, row_count: int, column_count: int) Instantiate a new path for a board with the given number of rows and columns.
  • get_position(self, index: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None
    Get the two dimensional board position corresponding to the given one dimensional path position. If the index does not correspond to a position on the board, return None.
  • get_index(self, position: tuple[int,int]) -> int | None
    Get the one dimensional path position corresponding to the given two dimensional board position. If the position does not occur on the board, return None.
  • get_length(self) -> int Get the length of this path.

Example:

>>> path = Path(5, 3)
>>> path.get_length()
15
>>> path.get_position(5)
(1, 0)
>>> path.get_index((1, 2))
3
>>> position = path.get_position(16)
>>> print(position, type(position))
None <class 'NoneType'>
>>> index = path.get_index((6, 2))
>>> print(index, type(index))
None <class 'NoneType'>

Task 14 SnakeGameModel()

The SnakeGameModel class is responsible for maintaining the game state, and applying game logic.

SnakeGameModel must implement the following methods:

  • __init__(self, tiles: list[Tile], entities: list[Entity], player: Player)
    Instantiates a new SnakeGameModel using the given tiles, entities, and player.
  • get_tiles(self) -> list[Tile]
    Return this model’s tiles.
  • get_tile(self, position: tuple[int, int]) -> Tile Return the Tile at the given position. You may assume the position is valid.
  • get_player(self) -> Player Return this model’s player instance.
  • entity_positions(self) -> dict[tuple[int, int], Entity]
    Returns a dictionary mapping the position of each non-player entity to the corresponding entity instance.
  • get_entity(self, position: tuple[int, int]) -> Entity | None Return the entity on the board at the given position, if no entity exists at that position, or if the position isn’t on the board, this method should return None.
  • remove_entity(self, entity: Entity) -> None Remove the given entity from the board. If the entity does not exist anywhere on the position, then nothing should happen.
  • has_lost(self) -> bool
    Return True if the player has lost the game per the Gameplay section, and False otherwise.
  • has_won(self) -> bool
    Return True if the player has won the game per the Gameplay section, and False otherwise.
  • move_player(self, steps: int) -> None
    Attempts to move the player forward by the given number of steps as per the rules given in the Gameplay section. After calling this method, effects related to stepping on entities or tiles should have been applied (that is to say, interaction logic should either be handled in this method, or any helper methods it calls).
  • take_turn(self) -> None Take one turn of the game. In each turn, dice is rolled, the number rolled is displayed, and then the player is moved forward by the number rolled. The player’s movement, including the effects of any snake or ladder encountered, is handled by move_player.
Caution

Some of these methods will become very long. You will likely benefit from adding extra helper methods to this class to help break up some of these long methods (adding helper methods also won’t hurt your style marks).

Example:

>>> tiles, entities, player = read_file('levels/level1.txt')
>>> model = SnakeGameModel(tiles, entities, player)
>>> model.get_tiles()
[[Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Exit()]]
>>> model.get_player()
Player((0, 0), 3, 15)
>>> model.entity_positions()
{(0, 3): HealthPotion((0, 3)),
 (1, 1): Snake((1, 1)),
 (1, 3): Ladder((1, 3), 3),
 (2, 2): RollPotion((2, 2)),
 (2, 4): Snake((2, 4)),
 (3, 0): Ladder((3, 0), 4),
 (3, 1): FancyPotion((3, 1))}
>>> model.has_won()
False
>>> model.has_lost()
False
>>> model.get_player().add_remaining_rolls(-20)
>>> model.get_player().get_remaining_rolls() <= 0
True
>>> model.has_won()
False
>>> model.has_lost()
True
>>> player = model.get_player()
>>> player.finish()
>>> model.has_won()
True
>>> model.has_lost()
True
>>> model.get_player()
Player((0, 0), 3, -5)
>>> model.get_tiles()
[[Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor()],
 [Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Floor(), Exit()]]
>>> model.get_tile((0,1))
Floor()
>>> model.entity_positions()
{(0, 3): HealthPotion((0, 3)),
 (1, 1): Snake((1, 1)),
 (1, 3): Ladder((1, 3), 3),
 (2, 2): RollPotion((2, 2)),
 (2, 4): Snake((2, 4)),
 (3, 0): Ladder((3, 0), 4),
 (3, 1): FancyPotion((3, 1))}
>>> ladder = model.get_entity((3,0))
>>> model.remove_entity(ladder)
>>> model.entity_positions()
{(0, 3): HealthPotion((0, 3)),
 (1, 1): Snake((1, 1)),
 (1, 3): Ladder((1, 3), 3),
 (2, 2): RollPotion((2, 2)),
 (2, 4): Snake((2, 4)),
 (3, 1): FancyPotion((3, 1))}
>>> model.move_player(3)
>>> model.entity_positions()
{(1, 1): Snake((1, 1)),
 (1, 3): Ladder((1, 3), 3),
 (2, 2): RollPotion((2, 2)),
 (2, 4): Snake((2, 4)),
 (3, 1): FancyPotion((3, 1))}
>>> model.get_player()
Player((0, 3), 4, -6)
>>> model.move_player(5)
>>> model.get_player()
Player((0, 0), 3, -7)

Task 15 Game()

Game represents a complete Snake Game. This class is responsible for handling input and output in order to play a game from start to end.

Note

One of the most important skills in programming is the ability to understand and use someone else’s code. You will be expected to be familiar with, and use, the functions and constants provided in support.py.

Game() should implement the following methods:

  • __init__(self, board_file: str)
    Constructs a new Game instance, including loading the game state from the specified file and constructing a corresponding SnakeGameModel.
  • display(self)
    Prints the current game state to the screen in a visually appealing format. The display should contain a rectangular grid of characters representing the board, as would be seen in a level file, followed by the player’s health and remaining rolls. The exact format expected by gradescope is given in the examples present in the gameplay/ folder.
  • play(self)
    Conducts a Snake Game from start to finish, following the Gameplay section. See the gameplay/ folder for example output from this method.

Task 16 main()

The purpose of the main function is to allow you to test your own code. The main function should be short and do exactly two things: make a new game and play it.

Assessment and Marking Criteria

This assignment assesses following course learning objectives:

  1. Apply program constructs such as variables, selection, iteration and sub-routines,
  2. Apply basic object-oriented concepts such as classes, instances and methods,
  3. Read and analyse code written by others,
  4. Analyse a problem and design an algorithmic solution to the problem,
  5. Read and analyse a design and be able to translate the design into a working program, and
  6. Apply techniques for testing and debugging.

There are a total of 100 marks for this assessment item.

Functionality

Your program’s functionality will be marked out of a total of 55 marks.

Your assignment will be put through a series of tests and your functionality mark will be proportional to the number of tests you pass. You will be given a subset of the functionality tests before the due date for the assignment.

You may receive partial marks within each section for partially working functions, or for implementing only a few functions.

Warning

You need to perform your own testing of your program to make sure that it meets all specifications given in the assignment. Only relying on the provided tests is likely to result in your program failing in some cases and you losing some functionality marks.

Note

Functionality tests are automated, so string outputs need to match exactly what is expected.

Your program must run in Gradescope, which uses Python 3.12. Partial solutions will be marked but if there are errors in your code that cause the interpreter to fail to execute your program, you will get zero for functionality marks. If there is a part of your code that causes the interpreter to fail, comment out the code so that the remainder can run. Your program must run using the Python 3.12 interpreter. If it runs in another environment (e.g. Python 3.8 or PyCharm) but not in the Python 3.12 interpreter, you will get zero for the functionality mark. Python versions newer than 3.12 will function correctly provided you do not use language features that are not introduced in the course.

Code Style

The style of your assignment will be assessed by a tutor. Style will be marked according to the style rubric provided with the assignment. The style mark will be out of 45.

Note

Style accounts for 45% of the marks available on this assignment

You are expected to follow the PEP-8 based style guidelines discussed in lectures. The key consideration in marking your code style is whether the code is easy to understand. There are several aspects of code style that contribute to how easy it is to understand code. In this assignment, your code style will be assessed against the following criteria:

  • Readability
    • Program Structure: Layout of code makes it easy to read and follow its logic. This includes using whitespace to highlight blocks of logic, and ensuring all lines are below 80 characters.
    • Descriptive Identifier Names: Variable, constant, and function names clearly describe what they represent in the program’s logic. Do not use Hungarian Notation for identifiers. In short, this means do not include the identifier’s type in its name, rather make the name meaningful (e.g. employee identifier).
    • Named Constants: Any non-trivial fixed value (literal constant) in the code is represented by a descriptive named constant (identifier).
  • Algorithmic Logic
    • Single Instance of Logic: Blocks of code should not be duplicated in your program. Any code that needs to be used multiple times should be implemented as a function.
    • Variable Scope: Variables should be declared locally in the function in which they are needed. Global variables should not be used.
    • Control Structures: Logic is structured simply and clearly through good use of control structures (e.g. loops and conditional statements).
  • Object-Oriented Program Structure
    • Classes & Instances: Objects are used as entities to which messages are sent, demonstrating understanding of the differences between classes and instances.
    • Encapsulation: Classes are designed as independent modules with state and behaviour. Methods only directly access the state of the object on which they were invoked. Methods never update the state of another object.
    • Abstraction: Public interfaces of classes are simple and reusable. Enabling modular and reusable components which abstract details.
    • Inheritance & Polymorphism: Subclasses are designed as specialised versions of their superclasses. Subclasses extend the behaviour of their superclass without re-implementing behaviour, or breaking the superclass behaviour or design. Subclasses redefine behaviour of appropriate methods to extend the superclasses’ type. Subclasses do not break their superclass’ interface.
  • Documentation:
    • Comment Clarity: Comments provide meaningful descriptions of the code. They should not repeat what is already obvious by reading the code (e.g. # Setting variable to 0). Comments should not be verbose or excessive, as this can make it difficult to follow the code. Comments must be written in English.
    • Informative Docstrings: Every function should have a docstring that summarises its purpose. This includes describing parameters and return values (including type information) so that others can understand how to use the function correctly.
    • Description of Logic: All significant blocks of code should have a comment (in English) to explain how the logic works. For a small function, this would usually be the docstring. For long or complex functions, there may be different blocks of code in the function. Each of these should have an in-line comment describing the logic.

Assignment Submission

You must submit your assignment electronically via Gradescope. You must use your UQ email address which is based on your student number (e.g. s4123456@student.uq.edu.au) as your Gradescope submission account.

When you login to Gradescope you may be presented with a list of courses. Select CSSE7030. You will see a list of assignments. Choose Assignment 2. You will be prompted to choose a file to upload. Do not select the option to submit using a git repository if it is presented to you. The prompt may say that you can upload any files, including zip files. You must submit your assignment as a single Python file called a2.py (use this name – all lower case), and nothing else. Your submission will be automatically run to determine the functionality mark. If you submit a file with a different name, the tests will fail and you will get zero for functionality. Do not submit any sort of archive file (e.g. zip, rar, 7z, etc.).

Upload an initial version of your assignment at least one week before the due date. Do this even if it is just the initial code provided with the assignment. If you are unable access Gradescope, make a post on Edstem immediately. Excuses, such as you were not able to login or were unable to upload a file will not be accepted as reasons for granting an extension.

When you upload your assignment it will run a set of the functionality autograder tests on your submission. It will show you the results of these tests. It is your responsibility to ensure that your uploaded assignment file runs and that it passes the tests you expect it to pass.

Late submission of the assignment will result in a deduction of 10% of the maximum possible mark per 24 hours from the deadline for up to 3 days. After 3 days (72 hours), you will receive a mark of zero. A one-hour grace period will be applied to the due time, after which time (16:00) your submission will be considered officially late and will receive a mark of 0. Do not wait until the last minute to submit your assignment, as the time to upload it may make it late. Multiple submissions are allowed and encouraged, so ensure that you have submitted an almost complete version of the assignment well before the submission deadline of 15:00.

Plagiarism and Reference of AI Use

To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. Plesae note that AI or MT tools are not required to be used and not recommended to be used as they may inhibit learning and introduce bugs into your code. You must always follow the referencing requirements. Please refer to the course AI Guideline. Failure to appropriately reference the resources (tools and information sources) used in your work may result in misconduct allegations against you. You must clearly reference any use of AI in each instance. You are encouraged to discuss the concepts behind the assignments but under no circumstances should you show your code to, or allow your code to be seen by, another student. You should not look at the code of any other student. You must sufficiently protect all electronic and paper copies of your code. All submitted code will be subject to electronic plagiarism and collusion detection. Assignments with no academic merit will be awarded a mark of zero.

Important

You must understand all code submitted and submit a PDF or WORD file in English alongside with your code submission. This file must provide detailed information about how the AI tools were used. Please refer to the AI Guideline for guidance on properly documenting interactions with AI.

You are encouraged to complete both parts A and B of the academic integrity modules before starting this assignment. Submitted assignments will be electronically checked for potential cases of plagiarism.

Assessment Interviews

Students must be able to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their submitted code independent of AI and machine-translation (MT) tools. The Course Coordinator reserves the right to require any student to participate in an oral examination regarding any assessment submission. During such an examination, students may be required to explain and/or modify their submitted code to demonstrate understanding. Assessment marks are provisional and subject to confirmation following any such examination. A student’s assessment mark may be adjusted, including reduced to zero, based on the level of understanding demonstrated during this examination.

During the examination, students may not use notes or modified code and must work exclusively from the code exactly as submitted. Failure to attend a scheduled examination without an approved reason, or failure to meaningfully participate, will be treated as unsatisfactory performance and may result in the relevant assessment mark being reduced, including to zero. Oral examinations will be scheduled on a case-by-case basis.
